5.text: eñeˊneñe are husband and wife. Although they constantly desire to meet,
5.as_typed: {en~e'nen~e} are husband and wife. Although they constantly desire to meet,

6.text: they are prevented, and obliged to pass each other in the air. Others say,

7.text: on the contrary, that, passing each other, they exchange mutual abuse.

8.text: The cold winds are said to be produced by giants who live on the border

9.text: of our earth, and spend their time shovelling snow with huge shovels made

10.text: of the shoulder-blades of whales. Sometimes the winds are said to have an

11.text: old mistress, who causes snow-storms by shaking the snow from her dwelling.

12.text: Thunder is said to be produced by the passing of the thunder-bird.

13.text: Others attribute it to the rattling noise made by girls playing on a spread seal-

14.text: skin. Rain is the urine of one of the girls. In one tale the lightning is

15.text: described as a one-sided man who drags his one-sided sister along by her

16.text: foot. She is intoxicated with fly-agaric. The noise caused by her back as it

17.text: strikes the floor of heaven is thunder, her urine is rain. Obsidian is said to

18.text: be the stone of the thunder, which falls from the sky in round balls, or

19.text: even in roughly chipped arrow-heads and lances. Perhaps the idea of stone

20.text: arrow-heads falling from the sky, so common in the Old World, is borrowed

21.text: from the Tungus or from the Russianized natives.
